title: Not numb
hookLine: how to hold the world's suffering, war and hunger, without going numb

lines: A HEADLINE AT ELEVEN AT NIGHT.
cards: Eleven at night. A phone lights up on the nightstand. A headline about a war.
Under it, a photo of a line of people waiting for bread. A thumb hovers for a second. Then it keeps moving: a recipe, a joke, a friend's new haircut.
Nobody in that moment is cruel. The heart has simply been asked to hold more than one heart can hold, and it closes the door a little. In everyday speech, that closing is called going numb.
Two old voices speak to keeping the door open without being flattened by what comes through.

teach.h: A CHILD AT THE EDGE OF A WELL.
teach.b: First, the Chinese teacher Mencius. In one passage he asks his listeners to imagine a person who suddenly sees a small child about to fall into a well. Anyone, he says, would feel a jolt of alarm and pity.
Not to win the parents' favor, not to be praised, not because the child's crying is annoying. Just that jolt.
Mencius calls that feeling a beginning of kindness, and some readers picture it as a sprout, the first shoot of a plant. A sprout is small, and it can be trampled. It can also be tended.
Second, what numbness is. Read with Mencius in mind, it isn't proof that someone has no heart.

teach.h: NUMB IS A SPROUT UNDER TOO MUCH WEATHER.
teach.b: It can be a sprout that got too much weather at once. The feeling doesn't die; it goes under, because it had nowhere to go. Third, a voice from Jewish tradition.

teach.h: NOT YOURS TO FINISH, NOT FREE TO LEAVE.
teach.b: In the Mishnah, in the collection called the Sayings of the Fathers, Rabbi Tarfon says something like this: the work is not yours to finish, and you are not free to walk away from it. Two halves, both needed.
The first half lifts the weight: no one person ends a war or a famine. The second half keeps the door open: walking away entirely isn't the answer either.
Fourth, the two together, each in its own place: Mencius says the feeling is a beginning; Tarfon says do your part without needing to finish the whole.

teach.h: GIVE THE FEELING ONE THING TO DO.
teach.b: The feeling stays alive when it is given one small thing to do.
A gift, a letter, learning a place's name and where it is on the map. Not everything. One thing.

how: Some people keep a small, regular gift for one distant cause, so hard news has somewhere to go; others hold a named place in prayer, or write to someone in a position to help.

o: feeling every far-off tragedy at full strength
shutting off the news so pain can't reach you
keeping the heart's first jolt alive with one small act

games.q: who said what about distant pain — tap the pairs.
p: a child at the edge of a well
not yours to finish, not free to leave
a feeling with nowhere to go

s: Mencius says people feel alarm for the child because they want praise
he says the opposite: not for favor, not for praise. just the jolt itself.
Rabbi Tarfon's saying says the work is not yours to finish
and in the same breath: you are not free to walk away from it.
in Mencius, the feeling of pity is a finished virtue
he calls it a beginning, which some readers picture as a sprout that can be tended or trampled.

games.q: a headline about hunger far away. you feel the jolt, then the urge to scroll on. which response matches Rabbi Tarfon's saying?
o: fix all of it, or it doesn't count.
do one part, without needing to finish the whole.
look away until it feels easier.
games.why: the work is not yours to finish, and you are not free to walk away from it. one act counts.

practice: Bring to mind one place where people are suffering now, say its name quietly, and notice whatever comes, a jolt, a tiredness, or nothing; any of it is fine.
Then choose one small act for that place: a gift, a message to someone who can help, one honest account read from there. If you pray, you can hold that place in prayer.

wordCard.voice: Not numb: keeping the heart's first jolt alive by giving it one small thing to do, without needing to finish the whole work. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese, from Mencius: the 'beginning' or sprout of a virtue. Legge's English puts it as 'principle'.

carryVoice: Your line: a beginning of kindness. One act is enough for today. That's day seven hundred forty-seven.
